title: NP-Complete
body:
The last step of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]], and a change of question.
[[Undecidability]] asked what can be computed *at all*; this asks what can be computed
*quickly*. An NP-complete problem has a perfectly good algorithm. The algorithm is just
exponential, and it looks like that is unavoidable.

This note also carries **P vs NP**, since the two are the same material.

## The classes

Both are defined over *decision* problems, questions with a yes/no answer, and both are
measured in [[Turing Machine]] steps, which is what makes them independent of language and
hardware.

| Class | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | solvable in polynomial time, $O(n^k)$ | sorting, shortest path, primality |
| **NP** | a proposed solution is *verifiable* in polynomial time | [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], SAT, subset sum |

The "N" is for **nondeterministic**, not "non-polynomial". The original definition is
"solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine", which guesses a solution
and checks it. Guess-and-check and verify-a-certificate are the same definition stated two
ways; see [[Nondeterminism]].

$P \subseteq NP$, obviously: if you can solve it fast you can check it fast by solving it
again. Whether the containment is strict is the open problem.

## P vs NP

> Is every problem whose solution can be *checked* quickly also one whose solution can be
> *found* quickly?

Nobody knows. It is a Clay Millennium Prize problem, and the consensus guess is $P \neq NP$,
on the grounds that thousands of NP-complete problems have been attacked independently for
fifty years with no polynomial algorithm found for any of them.

What hangs on it: if $P = NP$, then every NP-complete problem falls at once (that is what
completeness means), and most [[Public Key Cryptography|public-key cryptography]] dies, since
[[RSA]] depends on factoring being hard to invert and easy to check. Also, in a sense, mathematics gets easier, because
finding a proof of bounded length becomes as cheap as verifying one.

Note factoring itself is in NP but is **not known to be NP-complete**. It is one of the few
natural problems suspected to sit strictly between P and NP-complete.

## NP-complete

A problem $B$ is NP-complete when both hold:

1. $B \in NP$, and
2. **every** problem in NP reduces to $B$ in polynomial time (this half alone is *NP-hard*).

Condition 2 makes them the hardest problems in NP, and it makes them all the same problem
wearing different clothes. A polynomial algorithm for any single NP-complete problem gives one
for all of them, and proves $P = NP$.

**NP-hard** without condition 1 covers things that are at least as hard as NP but need not be
in NP, including undecidable problems. Halting is NP-hard and hopelessly worse than
NP-complete.

## Reduction

$A \leq_p B$ means there is a polynomial-time function converting instances of $A$ into
instances of $B$ with the same yes/no answer. Then a fast solver for $B$ gives a fast solver
for $A$, so $B$ is at least as hard as $A$.

To prove a new problem $B$ is NP-complete:

1. Show $B \in NP$ by describing a certificate and how to check it in polynomial time. This
   step is usually two lines, and people skip it and lose the marks.
2. Pick a known NP-complete problem $A$ and reduce **$A$ to $B$**, not $B$ to $A$.

The direction is the whole trick, and it is the same directional rule as the undecidability
reductions in [[Undecidability]]. Reducing $B$ to something known hard proves nothing about
$B$: it says $B$ is *no harder*, which is the opposite of what you want.

**Cook-Levin theorem** (1971) bootstrapped the whole field by proving SAT is NP-complete
directly, encoding the computation of an arbitrary nondeterministic TM as a boolean formula.
Everything since reduces from SAT, transitively.

## The standard list

SAT → 3-SAT → clique, vertex cover, independent set, [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], travelling
salesman, subset sum, knapsack, graph colouring, bin packing. Karp's original 21 problems came
out a year after Cook, and there are thousands now across scheduling, layout, and logistics.

## What you do about it

Exponential in the worst case does not mean give up:

- **Approximation**: accept a solution provably within a factor of optimal. Vertex cover has a
  simple 2-approximation.
- **Heuristics**: greedy, local search, simulated annealing. No guarantee, works well in
  practice.
- **Exact but pruned**: backtracking and branch-and-bound. Modern SAT solvers routinely handle
  millions of variables, which is a good reminder that worst case is not average case.
- **Restrict the input**: many NP-complete graph problems are polynomial on trees or on
  bounded-width graphs.

## Not the same as undecidable

| | Undecidable | NP-complete |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm exists? | No, ever | Yes |
| Problem | can never be solved | can be solved slowly |
| Example | halting problem | [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] |

## Not the same as hard-on-average

The neighbouring distinction, and the one [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] is built on.
NP-hardness is a **worst-case** statement: *some* instance is hard. A problem can be NP-complete
and still easy on almost every input you would ever generate, which is fine for a complexity class
and useless for a cipher.

| | NP-hardness | What cryptography needs |
|---|---|---|
| Guarantee | some instance is hard | a **randomly chosen** instance is hard |
| Case | worst case | average case |

That is why [[RSA]] rests on factoring and Diffie-Hellman on the
[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] even though **neither is known to be NP-complete**, and why nobody
is embarrassed about it. You do not get to pick your adversary's instance, you pick yours, and
yours is random. Proving $P = NP$ would break both; so would a fast factoring algorithm, without
touching $P$ vs $NP$ at all.

## Core Facts to Know

- **P**: decision problems solvable in polynomial time.
- **NP**: decision problems whose solutions can be *verified* in polynomial time.
- "N" is for nondeterministic, not non-polynomial.
- NP is equivalently "solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic [[Turing Machine]]".
- $P \subseteq NP$; whether $P = NP$ is open, and most believe not.
- A problem is **NP-complete** if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time.
- **NP-hard** drops the "in NP" requirement, so it includes undecidable problems.
- $A \leq_p B$: a polynomial-time mapping of $A$-instances to $B$-instances preserving the answer.
- To prove $B$ NP-complete: show $B \in NP$, then reduce a **known NP-complete problem to $B$**.
- Reducing in the wrong direction proves nothing.
- **SAT** was the first, by Cook-Levin, 1971.
- A polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem solves all of them and proves $P = NP$.
- Factoring is in NP but not known to be NP-complete.
- NP-complete is not undecidable: the algorithm exists, it is just too slow.
- **NP-hard is worst case; cryptography needs average case.** Not the same requirement, which is
  why [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] uses factoring and the [[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] rather than an
  NP-complete problem.
